# System review

## Scope and evidence

Review the complete CAVE system, fix issues found, improve its website and live
documentation, and propose and implement enhancements to the system itself.
Passing existing tests is a baseline, not proof that the review is complete.
Keep this scope intact across working sessions.

Use [Remaining review scope](#remaining-review-scope) and the
[Verification map](#verification-map) for the active scope. The evidence entries
record what individual passes established at that time. Earlier checkpoints
retain their original test counts and open-issue statements; later evidence may
supersede them. Recheck current code and the owning task before treating an old
checkpoint as an active defect or completion proof.

## Remaining review scope

- Review kernel invariants across core, parser, canonicalization, store, query,
  fusion, shapes, scenarios, and solvers. Exercise malformed input, transactions,
  temporal and sensitivity boundaries, provenance, and representative query costs.
  Current-export validation of omitted history is now explicit in both SQLite
  adapter contracts: malformed superseded rows unrelated to edges are omitted;
  full history rejects them, and current export rejects them when used to remap
  an edge. Repair restores the edge at the newer value without failed-read writes.
  Canonical graph emission now rejects sparse claim arrays before annotation
  callbacks instead of silently skipping holes. The regression preserves caller
  data and verifies corrected dense retry; both owning suites and builds pass.
  A deterministic composition regression now checks 4,928 parser-accepted
  subject/verb/payload/metadata combinations for complete semantic claim-field
  and edge preservation plus stable second emission. Both 73-test canonical
  suites pass; this finite corpus found no additional runtime defect.
  Annotation failure now has explicit shared-graph retry coverage: the original
  error propagates, later callbacks stop and fresh traversal restores the full
  order. Store annotations derive stable row IDs; sync preserves shared edges.
  Fusion's numeric fallback boundary is reviewed: validated finite binary64
  inputs bound operand exponents, while estimate count still governs work and
  temporary storage. Existing extreme-value, cancellation and rounding cases
  pass on both supported majors; the guide states caller-owned workload limits.
  Pure fusion evidence selection is now explicit: each supplied occurrence
  contributes weight; source contexts do not deduplicate evidence and a zero-
  confidence entry does not remove an earlier array entry. Callers select
  current evidence and account for repeated/correlated observations.
  MCP historical fusion now groups quantities using the same as-of alias
  graph as estimate selection. Later merges/retractions no longer regroup
  historical estimates; both MCP suites and installed-package checks pass.
  Fusion now reuses alias-component representatives within each read snapshot.
  A 100-estimate/100-link fixture falls from a 58.5 ms median to 4.4 ms with
  equal output hashes; 101 relevant MCP/protocol tests pass on both majors.
  This cache ends with each call and does not reuse state across snapshots.
  Query-record projection now has explicit combined-error recovery coverage:
  projection and release failures retain their order and original cause, an
  unprintable thrown value cannot mask them, and corrected projection retries
  inside the caller transaction before its rollback. Both 157-test suites pass.
  Query historical interpretation is reviewed across vocabulary, aliases and
  resolution policy. A combined regression preserves distinct winners before
  alias merge, after merge, after precedence change and after retraction.
  Direct cursor continuation now has explicit coverage for equal-valued claims,
  later revisions/retractions and cursor reuse in ordinary and exact-number
  pages. Old continuations retain claim IDs; fresh pages reflect current rows.
  Scenario overlay/evaluator handoff is now reviewed against source, guide and
  three current full-suite regressions per major. Overlays and vocabulary roll
  back before evaluator invocation; insertion failures suppress evaluation;
  pending or failed evaluators do not undo later base-store writes.
  Evaluator/result ownership is reviewed: inputs are frozen, evaluator outputs
  stay caller-owned until explicit recording, and returned recording artifacts
  are detached JSON snapshots. A regression now mutates that returned snapshot,
  confirms fresh reads retain stored content and retries idempotently unchanged.
  Scenario record identity and predecessor ordering are also reviewed. A
  missing-predecessor rejection now has explicit same-ID recovery coverage:
  history stays unchanged, the decision remains absent, and creating its
  recommendation permits recording followed by an existing-row retry.
  Optional governance text is now validated on recording and imported reads:
  recommendation rationale/authoredBy, decision rationale and action message
  reject non-string JSON values. Regressions preserve history on rejection and
  verify corrected reads plus omitted/empty text compatibility on both majors.
  Expanded assertions also cover immediate-predecessor use: malformed
  recommendations, decisions and actions block dependent records without writes;
  correcting the predecessor allows the same child ID and an idempotent repeat.
  Replay now rejects malformed expected model/backend identities before store
  reads, while valid mismatches retain explicit compatibility reasons. Fresh
  tests verify corrected requests, unchanged history and one-time getter capture.
  Artifact identifier serialization is reviewed against exact parsed-claim
  checks and current regressions for injected claims, altered subjects,
  successor IDs, one-time getter capture and historical ID ownership.
  Definition capture now traverses iteratively: a 20,000-level malformed
  overlay reaches classified validation instead of overflowing the JavaScript
  stack. Shared references, cycles, sparse arrays and getter order are preserved;
  capture still has no general memory or elapsed-time budget.
  Definition serialization now also runs before database access: cyclic,
  BigInt and excessively deep metadata reject as invalid definitions. The
  existing digest algorithm remains unchanged; corrected input can retry.
  Shape constraint validation now rejects binary stored unit tags instead of
  comparing them as units and reporting false violations. Shared validation

  CLI generation now has a regression proving binary unit errors preserve an

  Typed-client normalization is also reviewed: equivalent source declarations,

  Generated-reader snapshots now have direct mixed attribute/relation evidence:

  An independent Python datetime oracle now verifies 1,728 timestamps and 45

## Capture review disposition

The current capture implementation has no outstanding evidenced ownership or
failure/retry defect from this review. The table closes the listed requirements
against their current source and regression evidence; it does not claim complete
coverage of all JavaScript graphs or close the system-wide goal.

| Requirement | Current implementation and evidence | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| Use a stable model for validation and execution | `solve.ts` captures, validates and freezes before adapter use; `model.test.ts` and `workflow.test.ts` cover changing getters, options and awaited calls. Canonical/linear entrypoints validate their captured copies too. | Covered for the supported model contract. |
| Preserve graph ownership and sharing | `clone.ts` uses per-call maps and data-property creation; `clone.test.ts` covers cycles, sparse/named arrays, special keys and ignored properties. `explain.test.ts` and installed direct/solve checks verify mutations in either direction cannot affect another owner. | Covered, including removal of the redundant report copy. |
| Preserve native fallback behavior | Descriptor/proxy inspection chooses native cloning for the whole graph; direct tests cover getter count/order, mutation, containers and proxy rejection. | Native fallback remains intentional; it is not replaced with accessor evaluation in the portable path. |
| Fail without retaining partial captured state | Clone and result-proof tests retain original thrown identities, retry the same input and check detachment. The deep fallback case retries through portable copying after correction. | Covered. Caller getter side effects are not rolled back. |
| Validate captured result metadata and proof markers | `result.ts` captures before status/proof/reason/metadata validation; `result-proof.test.ts` exercises direct report, solve and solve-with-explanation boundaries. | Covered; semantic assignment checking remains a separate explanation/backend contract. |
| Measure representative copying costs and act on findings | Wide-model shared/distinct trials, diagnostic-list trials and owned-report assembly records retain values, hashes and source provenance. The primitive-preflight trial was rejected; two measured copy reductions were retained. | Measured families covered. Results do not establish universal time or memory limits. |
| State resource boundaries accurately | Solver capture guidance distinguishes model limits, initial capture, backend output limits, native stack depth, diagnostic count and process RSS. | Deliberate limits remain documented; absence of a universal capture budget is not an unimplemented requirement. |

At the capture audit, the named runtime and regression files matched the hashes
captured for the 3,268-test full runs on both Node majors. Later validation
diagnostic changes are verified separately below and do not alter capture ownership. The installed checkpoint also covers
current report ownership. Reopen a covered item for a concrete counterexample,
changed contract or materially different workload, rather than leaving the whole
capture category perpetually pending. Remaining validation, rendering,
standalone arithmetic, classification and native-backend reviews retain their
scope above.

Rejection and corrected submission tests suppress adapters until valid. | Covered. Objective array order remains semantic. |

Eight malformed-model cases and installed representative cases verify zero caller-method calls. | Covered for method overrides; arbitrary getter mutation is not converted into a new snapshot guarantee. |

Shared expressions retain occurrence charges; enum indexes reset each call. | Covered for the named limits and tested ordering, not every allocation before or during validation. |

## Expression-key construction disposition

This review covers private ordered syntax keys used by local explanation reuse.
It does not add an overall text-byte allowance or hard report deadline. Those
remain documented resource boundaries, not implicit requirements for this cache.

| Requirement | Inspected implementation and evidence | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preserve evaluation-sensitive identity | `expression-key.ts` emits node kind, literal sort/representation, enum domain, variadic arity and ordered children. JSON token encoding escapes embedded text; fixed-arity operators delimit their children through the syntax. Current regressions compare ordered failures and 298 predicate shapes across assignments and budgets. | Covered for validated model syntax and the tested isolation corpus. |
| Keep reuse local to one calculation | `feasible` creates the string table, structural result map and identity WeakMap. `evaluation` caches Boolean outcomes or reasons, with fresh maps on later calls. Changed-assignment/budget and declaration-metadata regressions pass. | Covered; no garbage-collection timing promise. |
| Avoid rebuilding keys for identical captured roots | `evaluation` checks its WeakMap before key construction. Distinct roots retain structural fallback. The shared-predicate record includes output hashes and shared/distinct controls. | Implemented and measured; no universal speedup claim. |
| Account for traversal and storage | The iterative builder pushes each child occurrence once, appends one token per occurrence and joins once. It does not concatenate complete subtree keys repeatedly. Validation charges expanded occurrences; pending nodes, tokens, final keys and interned text still occupy memory. | Construction structure reviewed. Text scanning, hashing and runtime allocation costs are not a hard resource budget. |
| Examine representative text and reuse costs | Retained variable/enum-name, shared-root and exponent-padding trials distinguish compact references, occurrence counts, numeric spelling and complete-report timings. The current key-builder hash matches the retained long-name checkpoint. | Measured families covered; earlier full-report timings remain point-in-time observations rather than current whole-source performance claims. |

Existing tests cover deep nesting, ordering, escaping, omitted fields, changing getters, shared graphs and cycle repair without mutation. | Covered for finite JSON and the tested recovery boundary. |

The retained million-character diagnostic trial measures the implemented fixed-escape reuse. | Measured and documented; no independent rendering byte/time cap is promised. |

## Standalone Exact disposition

Reviewed all five exported operations in `exact.ts` and the shared integer GCD
helper. This closes their inspected input, normalization, comparison and zero
contracts and representative cost review. It does not close intermediate sum/
product evaluation elsewhere or promise unrestricted inputs can be processed
within a universal time/memory budget.

| Requirement | Current implementation and evidence | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accept exact input types and complete syntax | `integer` requires primitive safe-integer numbers or full integer text. Decimal parsing requires complete syntax and safe-integer exponents; rational containers are non-null objects. Coercible/callable, trailing-line-break and malformed-preview regressions pass. | Covered; standalone calls do not inherit model limits. |
| Normalize signs, zero and common factors | `rational` and `fromBigInts` reject zero denominators, produce positive denominators and reduced decimal-string components, and preserve zero as 0/1. Independent small trial-division/value checks, sign cases and large Fibonacci factors exercise these paths. | Covered by source inspection and independent arithmetic checks. |
| Preserve exact decimal values | Decimal scaling cancels trailing powers of ten before allocation; zero validates the exponent before returning 0/1. Decimal/BigInt reference cases cover signs and scales, with representability failure followed by successful retry. | Covered; safe exponent syntax does not guarantee a representable expansion. |
| Order both operands exactly | `compare` normalizes both operands, uses canonical sign/magnitude shortcuts and falls back to BigInt cross-products. The finite signed-fraction corpus compares outcomes with direct cross-products, including opposing numerator/denominator orders. | Covered; runtime allocation remains input-dependent. |
| Check zero without unnecessary expansion | `isZero` validates integer fields and denominator even for zero, and validates decimal exponents without constructing powers. Large text and safe-exponent boundary tests check both answers and avoided parsing. | Covered; a zero check is not a representability check for later normalization. |
| Preserve GCD correctness through batching | Matrix steps preserve the GCD; full-width ordered progress is checked before accepting a batch, otherwise a Euclidean remainder advances. Deterministic sign/zero/size/factor cases agree with ordinary Euclid, including large Fibonacci inputs. Retained strategy and normalization trials record measured costs. | Implemented and measured with explicit finite-workload limits. |

Six named oracle/boundary regressions pass in both current 225-test solver logs,
alongside the other numeric type, normalization and diagnostic regressions.
Current inspection found no new defect or justified optimization. Reopen a
covered item for a concrete counterexample, changed API contract or materially
different workload. Intermediate expression arithmetic, validation text costs,
linear classification, native deadlines and other system areas remain active.

## Z3 runtime-lifecycle disposition

Reviewed lazy initialization, runtime queue/close/create ownership and the private
deadline, cleanup, release and worker-shutdown helpers. This covers the adapter's
cooperative lifecycle contract. Native solver internals, arbitrary stall recovery,
hard process deadlines and model/result translation are separate scopes.

| Requirement | Current implementation and evidence | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Serialize native requests and prevent use during shutdown | `runtime.ts` queues work through a settling tail; close marks the runtime unavailable before enqueueing teardown. Simultaneous solve and close/reopen tests exercise state isolation and replacement ownership. | Covered for the runtime queue contract. |
| Request cancellation and preserve failures | The deadline helper repeats interrupts until settlement, retains the first interrupt failure, combines it with check failure and clears its timer in `finally`. Fake-timer tests cover ignored interrupts, failure values and timer cleanup. | Covered; no forced native termination promise. |
| Release owned solver resources after operations | `withRelease` awaits the operation and attempts release once, retaining operation/release errors and cause ordering. Runtime feasibility, core and optimization paths use it. | Covered by source inspection and success/failure/retry tests. |
| Defer native reference deletion during active checks | Cleanup wrappers queue decrements/context deletion while checks are active and drain all releases at the final settlement, preserving failures. Rejection, concurrent checks and subsequent checks have tests. | Covered for the wrapped operations used by CAVE. |
| Keep worker handlers until exit acknowledgment | `closeWorkers` awaits every termination attempt, handles workers added by pending messages and clears the pool only after successful exit processing. Failures retain handlers and original/aggregate causes. | Covered by worker lifecycle tests; failed shutdown stays failed. |
| Verify live timeout recovery | An actual 1 ms pigeonhole timeout is followed by a satisfiable solve on the same runtime with assignment and earlier-result preservation assertions. | Both current 70-test Z3 suites pass; finite native workload evidence. |

Eight named lifecycle tests pass in both current Z3 suite logs, alongside the
failure permutations and live deadline test. `close()` waits behind pending
checks, so an unresponsive native check can also keep shutdown pending. That is
an explicit cooperative boundary, not an unimplemented hard-deadline feature.
The historical long-stall root cause remains unproven; these checks do not
retroactively explain it. Reopen covered lifecycle rows for concrete new failures
or contract changes. Adapter translation and the rest of the system retain their
review scope.

## Federated output rollback disposition

Reviewed direct `withFederatedSource` and declared query replay through query
projection and output. Both capture JSON records while temporary claims exist,
roll back before stdout, and retain mapping-failure exit status. Projection
exceptions also escape through transaction rollback before any JSON is printed.

| Requirement | Current implementation and evidence | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preserve temporary source metadata in returned records | Projection happens inside the transaction, before rollback. Existing direct/declared tests decode contexts and run provenance for successful and partial mappings. | Covered. |
| Restore history after projection failure | Identity/provenance corruption tests compare all five claim/annotation tables and verify a repaired retry. | Covered. |
| Restore history despite output and close failures | Expanded direct/declared query cases compare all five tables after both failures, including unprintable diagnostics. No temporary bookkeeping or metadata survives. | Covered on Node 26 and 24. |
| Reject stale declared replay | Replay compares the snapshot baseline inside its transaction and retries discovery up to the configured limit. | Covered by end-to-end writer-during-fetch tests: fresh replay, three-attempt exhaustion, unchanged writer history and quiet recovery. |

The output rollback and concurrent declaration replay boundaries now have
end-to-end coverage. Two deterministic writer-during-fetch cases exercise the
actual query entrypoint with separate live database connections, including fresh
results, retry exhaustion without JSON, exact five-table writer-history
preservation and successful quiet retry. The README now explains the three
attempts and distinguishes stored declaration changes from remote-content
changes. These tests do not establish an atomic remote-data snapshot or close
unrelated connector and kernel review work. No executable behavior changed.

subsequent quiet query succeeds without adding history.

### Competing Z3 objectives now prove declaration-priority behavior

### Malformed automation redeclaration preserves rearming semantics

Reviewed `declareAutomations` and `retractAutomation` after the stored-body
diagnostic fix. Added a regression for empty/nonempty binary current bodies:
failed retraction leaves the complete claim table unchanged; a valid declaration
appends a replacement, lists normally and is idempotent when repeated. An event
from before that replacement does not fire, while a new event fires exactly once.
Retraction of the valid replacement succeeds and hides the automation. The
original malformed historical row remains byte-for-byte unchanged.

operation but creates a new arming point, does not replay older events and does
not repair malformed history. It also explains why retraction of a malformed
current body can fail atomically before a valid replacement restores that path.

trigger selection, before advancing the watermark. Only fully prepared batches

### Six-step denominator probing avoids delayed shared-factor growth

Added a delayed-shared family (13N, 21N) to the existing sum benchmark. Unlike
3N/5N, its GCD requires six Euclidean remainders. The previous four-step probe
falls back to a denominator containing N twice. Compared four, eight and six
steps using isolated copies of all solver sources; timed trials did not overlap
builds/tests. Full trials pass 48 workloads and 96 exact magnitude controls per
variant and Node major, retaining existing shared, nearby and Fibonacci families.

Initial eight-step results suggested a useful gain but mixed coprime costs.
Six alternating paired runs per major confirmed the gain. A smaller six-step
candidate is the first tested bound that completes this factor: at 20,000
digits, median-of-run-median explanation times for add/subtract change from
7.291/7.117 to 6.132/6.051 ms on Node 26, and 7.604/7.433 to 6.242/6.291 ms on
Node 24. Paired Fibonacci controls range from 0.8% faster to 1.9% slower. Selected
six to retain this gain with less speculative coprime work than eight; this is
a measured tradeoff, not a universal speedup or bound on remainder time.

(`/tmp/cave-six-probe-before.log`) and passes after, requiring the shared factor
to occur only once rather than be squared. Expanded existing exact-value and

### Viewer runtime server errors initiate command cleanup

An analogous lifecycle scan found no additional direct filesystem watchers, but
found that `runServe` waited only for abort after HTTP startup. The server's
startup error listener rejects an already-settled promise after binding, so a
runtime error did not wake command cleanup. A regression reproduced the command
remaining pending after that event (`/tmp/cave-view-runtime-before.log`).

Replaced the abort-only wait with an owned stop boundary registered before the
startup announcement. Runtime error events append their original values to the
existing ordered error list and wake the command; the handler stays installed
through listener and store cleanup, then both error and abort subscriptions are
removed. The wait promise resolves rather than rejecting outside an awaited
path. Existing explicit cancellation and combined cleanup-error behavior remain
covered by the owning suite.

### Exponent padding distinguishes numeric expansion from syntax text size

Inspected ordered syntax-key construction and numeric-size accounting. Numeric
literal spelling remains part of evaluation identity, while `numericDigits`
counts coefficient and expanded numerator/denominator size, excluding exponent
spelling. Leading zero padding can therefore enlarge syntax text without
increasing the numeric allowance. This is consistent with the existing expansion
contract; silently redefining that allowance as an input-text budget would change
accepted models. No runtime change is justified by the observed bounded trial.

Added `scripts/solver-exponent-padding-bench.mjs` and preserved complete reports
in `benchmarks/exponent-padding-review.json`. Fresh sequential children on Node
24.21.0 and 26.8.1 test 1, 1,024 and 65,536 exponent zeros in a three-node
predicate. Each rejects `maxNumericDigits: 3`, accepts 4, reports satisfaction
and produces an identical full report hash across all sizes and both runtimes.
Key lengths are 60, 1,083 and 65,595 UTF-16 code units; the harness asserts the
exact linear growth. Four full-report samples discard the first; largest-case
medians are 1.407 ms on Node 24 and 1.450 ms on Node 26. Construction, key
measurement and assertions are outside report timing, but included in process
peak RSS. External 60-second/256 MB controls establish no library ceiling.

The solver guide and benchmark index now explain and link this dimension.
Reviewed documentation projections: the website imports the guide; no public
API, CLI behavior, language semantics or book examples changed. Raw outputs are
`/tmp/cave-exponent-padding24.json` and `/tmp/cave-exponent-padding26.json`.

before store release. Ordinary reported pass failures remain retryable.

### Soft-weight formatting preserves exact fractions after numeric preflight

Traced soft weights through `Validate.model`, `Exact.rational`, explanation
projection, Z3 `rationalText` and the installed binding's `addSoft`. `Solve.run`
charges both fraction components before exact positivity validation and backend
invocation. The adapter normalizes the fraction and submits its two components
as `numerator/denominator`; the binding passes that string to the native API.
There is no repeating-decimal expansion or JavaScript-number conversion on this
path. Formatting copies normalized components; reduction and native optimization
remain distinct resource costs outside this formatting conclusion.

Added a real-backend regression using weights `1/3` and
`(2^256 + 1)/(3 * 2^256)`. Their binary64 conversions compare equal, but swapping
the stronger weight between opposed Boolean preferences reverses the chosen
assignment on the same runtime. Both results are optimal. The existing numeric
budget regression checks pre-reduction charging for `12/30`, accepts exactly
four digits and rejects three; its assertions and passing entries were inspected
in both current full-suite logs.

### Z3 deadline interrupt failures stay with the pending check

escaped the solve promise. Four new cases reproduced this in
`/tmp/cave-deadline-interrupt-before.log` with successful/rejected checks and
interrupts throwing `undefined` or an unprintable object.

The callback now retains the first interrupt failure and continues cooperative
cancellation retries without accumulating errors. The helper waits for the
native check to settle before reporting that failure, keeping the caller's
solver/optimizer `finally` cleanup after pending work. If the check also rejects,
an `AggregateError` retains the check error first and as cause, followed by the
first interrupt failure. A settled check with an interrupt error rejects with
that original value. The existing adapter failure boundary handles this result.

The regressions verify no timer exception escapes, the operation remains pending
after its first interrupt failure, a second failure does not replace the first,
a third interrupt settles the check, timers stop and a fresh check has no stale
error state. All seven deadline tests pass after the fix. Complete Z3 suites
pass on Node 26.8.1 and 24.21.0 with 56 tests each and no failures, cancellations,

### Fusion reuses alias components within each read snapshot

traversal, even when all estimates referred to the same component. A new
reproducible `scripts/fusion-grouping-bench.mjs` fixture uses 100 source-attributed
estimates of one quantity with a 100-link alias chain. On Node 26.8.1/macOS
arm64, the pre-change five-call median was 58.516 ms.

returned by its first traversal. The map belongs to one `cave_fuse` invocation
inside its read snapshot and is discarded afterward. Current-time and
historical lookup retain their existing selection paths. This avoids repeated
traversal without a cross-call cache, store API change or stale alias reuse.

### Scenario definition serialization rejects before database access

Binding previously computed its definition digest after store reads and overlay
materialization. Extra caller metadata participates in that digest but is not
part of field validation. Cyclic, BigInt or excessively deep metadata could
therefore fail late with native serialization errors. The new closed-store
regression first failed with `database is not open`, confirming database access
preceded this validation.

Binding now computes the same digest immediately after field validation,
classifies serialization failures as `invalid-definition`, and reuses the
computed digest in the result. The serializer and accepted digest bytes are
unchanged. Regression cases cover cycles, BigInt and 20,000 nested objects on
closed and live stores, unchanged history after rejection, corrected-input
retry and explanation compatibility. This does not add support for arbitrary
serialization depth or a general resource budget. Explanation record cloning
remains a separate runtime serialization boundary.

`/tmp/cave-scenario-digest24.log` and `/tmp/cave-scenario-digest26.log`.

map. Object entries are captured at frame entry, preserving sibling-getter
reads before descent; shared references/cycles reuse the same owned copies.

getter order, cycle identity, sparse-array holes/length, own `__proto__` data,
null object prototypes and an unfrozen caller. The deep malformed overlay now
fails with `invalid-definition` before attempting database access.

### Linear classification folds wide operand results

The affine classifier previously retained every sum/product operand result in
an array, then scanned it again (`every` and, for products, `filter`). It now
folds linearity and constant/variable counts while still evaluating every
operand. This removes fan-out-proportional temporary classification arrays
without changing repeated-variable counting or defined-divisor requirements.

The sequential 25,000-operand trial uses one variable and a shared constant,
one warmup and seven complete calls per operation. Product medians improve
33.049 to 31.793 ms on Node 24.21.0 and 31.550 to 30.308 ms on Node 26.8.1;
sum medians are essentially unchanged. The artifact records raw samples,
source hashes and workload limitations in
`benchmarks/linear-classification-fold-review.json`; the reusable entrypoint is
`scripts/linear-classification-bench.mjs`. Peak memory was not measured.

All 197 owning solver tests pass on both supported majors, including the
constant-sign arithmetic comparisons, undefined-subexpression checks, shared
numeric budgets, raised-depth traversal and repeated-factor classification
(`/tmp/cave-linear-fold-test24.log`, `/tmp/cave-linear-fold-test26.log`). The
workspace TypeScript build passes (`/tmp/cave-linear-fold-build.log`). Updated
the solver reference and benchmark index; there is no public API or book

### Balanced Rolldown runtime calls do not establish native cleanup

A temporary preload wrapped the cached Rolldown 1.2.6 binding before Vite import
and recorded runtime starts/shutdowns with call stacks. Cold-cache Node 26.8.1
trial 20 timed out after 19 natural exits. The failure emitted `closed: true`,
then reported the same referenced native async handle with all three runtime
starts paired with shutdowns (config bundle, scan, dependency bundle). Evidence:
`/tmp/cave-runtime-trace26.json` and `/tmp/cave-runtime-trace26-19.log`.
Twelve subsequent complete website suites with that preload each passed 146
tests (`/tmp/cave-runtime-suite26.json`); no full-workspace pass is implied.

The versioned upstream `crates/rolldown_binding/src/lib.rs` confirms that the
exported runtime functions only act under WASM plus `tokio_unstable`; they are
no-ops on native macOS. This rejects adding a runtime release as a native fix
and redirects investigation to Node-API callback/future and bundler cleanup.
The existing Vite patch and cold-cache regression remain unchanged. Reviewed
the dependency guide and bug record together; no public API, website copy or
book contract changed.


### Shutdown diagnostics distinguish returned close from process liveness

The remaining failure reproduced without tracing on the fifth repeated website
suite. Twelve traced cold-cache probes passed; those successes did not establish
resolution. Diagnostics delayed until a timeout reproduced the suite failure
again. Crucially, moving the result report after `await server.close()` showed
`closed: true` before the child still reached its 15-second parent timeout.
The close promise was no longer the pending operation in that failure.

A native sample shows the main thread idle in `uv__io_poll`. The delayed handle
report identifies inactive standard input/output/error pipes and a separate
active, referenced native libuv async handle. Thus the earlier inference that
an absent diagnostic timer indicated a blocked event loop was rejected: that
timer had been cleared when close returned. Logs include
`/tmp/cave-vite-close-completed26-2.log`,
`/tmp/cave-vite-close-handles26-3.log` and
`/tmp/cave-vite-close-native26-4.sample`.

A temporary patch reordered optimizer cancellation after scan completion to
cover work created by a finishing scan. Its repeated suite still failed on the
third trial (`/tmp/cave-vite-close-ordered26-2.log`), so it was reverted. The
existing two-line promise-settlement patch remains unchanged. Rolldown runtime
acquisition/release is an investigation lead, not a proven leaking allocation.

The retained probe now reports only after close returns and adds delayed,
non-liveness-extending diagnostics for a lingering process; the regression
requires both the closed marker and exit zero. The parent timeout is unchanged.
DOCUMENTATION.md review updated the bug and dependency guide with this more
precise failure boundary. Changeset metadata and selected whitespace checks
pass. Reliable shutdown, full integration and the broader review remain open.

closed; client plugins and pending optimized-dependency transforms did not.

never settled. Vite's existing closed-optimizer branch already resolves the
current and queued promises, but that branch need not run after cancellation.

promises after optimizer cancellation. Vite is pinned exactly to 8.3.0, with

successful process exit or disable optimization. The cold-cache regression
in `website/test/vite-close.test.ts` failed before the patch on Node 24 after

cache and requires process exit zero after five successful route/worker
requests. The diagnostic remains available for future version comparisons.

### Projection construction reuses context and tag statements

Scoped copying called source.toClaim for every row, preparing identical context
and tag queries each time. Construction now prepares those two queries once per
projection and passes each row's fetched metadata to the same Row.toClaim
decoder. Identity validation, exact provenance copying, per-row reads, snapshot
and cleanup behavior remain in place; no global statement cache was introduced.

The unchanged entity projection benchmark ran in five fresh processes per Node
major before and after the edit, sequentially and alone. For 1,000 claims, cold
construction medians fell from 89.60 to 81.68 ms on Node 24.21.0 and 86.16 to
79.94 ms on Node 26.8.1. Provenance-invalidated medians fell from 86.82 to
81.52 ms and 87.13 to 79.71 ms respectively; cached medians remained roughly
14–15 ms. Every timed result matched the source baseline, and exact provenance
and cache build counts passed. `benchmarks/view-projection-statements-review.json`
retains all samples, hashes and method. Fixed run order and small sample count
limit causal precision; no general latency or resource bound is claimed.

All 165 view/report tests pass on both majors. The authored-text, complete-row,
entity-response and provenance fidelity replay also passes native SQLite and
sql.js on both. Typecheck, ten documentation checks, site build, all 12 packed

### Current projection costs distinguish construction from cached reads

The new `scripts/view-projection-bench.mjs` measures complete public entity
views for 100 and 1,000 claims with six stored provenance entries each. It
compares every result with the restricted source view, verifies exact copied
provenance, and asserts one initial projection build plus one rebuild after a
provenance-only edit. Five cached calls reuse the initial projection. All
assertions and seeding are outside the timers.

Sequential runs alone on Node 24.21.0 and 26.8.1, with identity validation and
exact attribution copying enabled, measure 1,000-claim cold projection reads at
92.21/86.29 ms, cached medians at 14.56/13.89 ms, and provenance-invalidated reads
at 86.68/90.23 ms. Cold and invalidated times are single observations; cached
values are medians of five. Full samples, method and source hashes are retained
in `benchmarks/view-projection-fidelity-review.json`. These are in-memory native
SQLite measurements, not HTTP/browser latency, a before/after cost attribution,
or a general performance bound.

The first driver used search and its cache-build assertion correctly failed:
search reads the source directly inside a snapshot rather than constructing a
projection. The final driver measures entity views, and the view guide now
makes that distinction explicit. This was a workload-selection correction,
not a runtime defect. The final measured script also asserts its fixture's six
provenance entries per claim.

### Restricted HTTP views reject corrupt claim identity

from stored contexts, as the view guide describes. The same row-shaping path
revealed an identity validation gap: restricted views read the source directly
and still returned arbitrary stored keys and decoded unchecked transaction
prefixes, bypassing the new sensitivity-projection checks. The HTTP regression
reproduced status 200 where identity corruption required failure.

link. Real HTTP GET/HEAD regressions exercise entity, history, lineage and search
with a corrupted key, a different valid transaction UUID and trailing junk.

### Report dates require valid stored transaction identity

The report date decoder read the timestamp prefix of `row.tx` without first
validating its canonical UUIDv7 form or agreement with the claim's row ID.
A different valid UUID could therefore produce a false citation date, while
sensitivity projections silently replaced the stored transaction with the row
ID during copying. The new regression failed with “Missing expected exception”
before the fix (`/tmp/cave-report-tx-before.log`).

Citation rendering and sensitivity projection construction now require a
canonical lowercase UUIDv7 row ID with `tx = id`. Mismatches abort with the
source row ID before rendering a date or copying metadata. The regression
exercises a different valid UUID, uppercase transaction text and trailing junk
at public/internal/restricted ceilings, verifies unchanged source rows on
failure, and verifies exact original reports after repair.

All 163 view/report tests pass on Node 24.21.0 and 26.8.1, including existing
expanded-year date coverage. Typecheck, ten documentation tests, site build,
all 12 packed public-package smoke checks and bundled documentation links pass.
Installed report smoke covers mismatched and malformed transactions at all
three ceilings and corrected retry. Logs use `/tmp/cave-report-tx-`.

The view README and storage/query specification describe the transaction
identity requirement. Valid report output and public types remain unchanged;

### Reports and projections reject corrupted citation identities

A report could print an arbitrary corrupted stored claim key in restricted
mode. Narrower sensitivity projections instead copied decoded claims into a
new store, silently reconstructing keys and hiding the mismatch. The new
regression failed with “Missing expected exception” before the fix. Both paths
could undermine the documented link from a citation to its source history.

Report citation rendering now compares the decoded claim's semantic key with
the stored key before constructing its footnote. Sensitivity projection
construction validates all included row keys before inserting the copied
claims. Mismatches abort rendering with the affected source row ID. The shared
report fixture checks public/internal/restricted modes, unchanged source rows
on failure, exact original reports after repair, and an unaffected public report
when the corrupt row is restricted and omitted.

excluded-row assertion passes in a final focused rerun on both. Typechecking,

`/tmp/cave-report-key-`; the before-fix log records the reproduced failure.

and public types remain unchanged: valid citation rendering is preserved.

rendering citations; no new performance bound is claimed. Full workspace and

### Historical export keys cannot redirect current relationships

A scratch replay demonstrated that corrupting an old `parent EXISTS` row's
stored key to the key of `other EXISTS` caused current-only export to attach
`WHEN child` to `other`. The selected current claims themselves were healthy,
so annotated export's existing included-row key checks did not detect the
misdirected historical edge. The initial regression failed with a missing
expected exception (`/tmp/cave-export-remap-before.log`).

Before using a historical endpoint to map onto a selected current row, export
now reconstructs its claim and contexts and checks the semantic key against
the stored key. Both plain and annotated current exports reject a mismatch
with the historical row ID and retained cause. Successful checks are cached
per endpoint within the export snapshot. Direct current endpoints keep their
existing path; omitted historical rows are not comprehensively certified.
The shared native/Wasm regression confirms rejection without modifying claims
or edges and restores the exact original export after repairing the fixture.

All 579 store/sync/website tests pass on Node 24 and Node 26
(`/tmp/cave-export-remap{24,26}-final.log`). Typecheck, all 12 installed-package
smoke checks including the new historical remapping/recovery case, all ten
documentation checks and the site build pass. The full production-browser
suite passes all 144 tests in 3.2 minutes against the rebuilt worker, with
32 documentation pages and 399 links and no missing targets or duplicate IDs.
Logs are `/tmp/cave-export-remap-{typecheck,packed,docs,site,links,full-browser}.log`.
The earlier 3,173-test full workspace checkpoints predate this runtime fix.

### Canonical preparation reuses shared expressions within one model

Capture preserves shared object references, but canonical preparation previously
created a separate conversion cache for each hard constraint, soft constraint
and objective. It now shares that cache within one captured model operation.
Equal but distinct objects are not merged. Validation still visits and charges
every occurrence before preparation, and a fresh public call starts a new cache.
The regression compares shared and JSON-expanded models, checks all 13 node
occurrences and rejection at a 12-node limit, then mutates the original graph
and verifies changed identity without affecting the independent expanded model.

The unchanged serialization driver uses 5,000 constraints sharing one ten-literal
Boolean expression. Four calls per sequential fresh process, with the first
excluded from the median, show Node 24 time changing from 223.263 to 80.950 ms
and lifetime peak RSS from 261,040 to 190,624 KiB. Node 26 changes from 195.311
to 77.190 ms and 211,584 to 193,328 KiB. Every call retains the same 2,604,001
bytes and SHA-256. No tests or builds ran concurrently with these measurements.
Construction and assertions are outside timing but inside lifetime memory;
256 MiB old-space is not a process-memory cap. These observations cover this
shared flat graph only, not unshared inputs or general resource guarantees.
Samples and source hashes are in
`benchmarks/canonical-preparation-sharing-review.json`.

### Full canonical serialization joins bounded token batches

Full serialization previously retained one array entry per JSON token before
joining the complete output. It now joins the same complete-token batches used
by digest hashing. The common generator flushes after reaching 65,536 UTF-16
code units; individual larger tokens remain intact. Canonical ordering, output
bytes, before/after-capture validation and public signatures are unchanged.
This reduces intermediate array overhead without removing the complete output
string, canonical model or individual-token allocations.

A sequential fresh-process trial on each runtime serializes 5,000 constraints
with ten Boolean literals apiece, using four calls and excluding the first from
the timing median. Both variants produce the same 2,604,001 bytes and SHA-256.
Node 24 median time changes from 242.430 to 225.194 ms, with lifetime peak RSS
324,720 to 256,992 KiB. Node 26 changes from 205.307 to 186.834 ms and 240,528 to
205,568 KiB. No builds or tests ran concurrently with the trials. Construction
and result checks are outside the timer but included in lifetime RSS; the
256 MiB V8 old-space setting does not bound process memory. The retained driver
and source/sample artifact are `scripts/solver-canonical-serialization-bench.mjs`
and `benchmarks/canonical-serialization-batch-review.json`. This flat workload
provides no universal speed or memory guarantee.

### Canonical ordering matches complete text across escaped enum values

A new model regression checks canonical ordering using complete rendered JSON
strings, independently of the production lazy token comparator. Eleven models
rotate enum comparisons across prefix strings, quotes, backslashes, newlines,
accented text, emoji, lone high/low surrogates and two values sharing 65,536
characters. Each model contains nested `and`/`or` expressions and `eq`/`neq`
comparisons. Parsed canonical output must order every commutative operand by its
complete JSON text. Reversing all those operands must preserve serialized bytes
and SHA-256 identity; both digest variants must equal hashing the complete UTF-8
serialization.

### Batched canonical digests avoid complete serialized-model allocation

Both public and report-owned digest paths previously assembled the complete
canonical JSON string before hashing it. They now consume the existing canonical
token stream in batches, flushing once accumulated length reaches 65,536 UTF-16
code units without splitting individual tokens. Public serialization remains
unchanged; public digest still validates before capture and validates the owned
model afterward. Canonical model preparation and oversized individual tokens
remain allocation boundaries, so batching is not a general memory limit.

The regression compares public and report digests with SHA-256 of serialized
UTF-8 at four sizes around the batch threshold. It includes supplementary Unicode,
escaped quotes/backslashes/newlines and a lone surrogate in allowed enum values.
An initial fixture incorrectly put Unicode in a variable ID and was rejected by
the existing ID grammar; the corrected fixture keeps IDs valid. All 356
solver/Z3/scenario tests then pass on both supported Node majors
(`/tmp/cave-stream-digest{24,26}-final.log`), including existing capture and
identity regressions. Workspace typecheck passes.

no concurrent builds or tests. Largest-case full-report medians change from
168.384 to 146.083 ms on Node 24 and 115.340 to 90.960 ms on Node 26. Lifetime
peak RSS changes from 497,216 to 118,672 KiB and 440,896 to 123,296 KiB. The
smallest control is slightly slower (26.126 to 26.378 ms; 21.381 to 23.861 ms).
benchmarks/explanation-streamed-digest-review.json retains all four-call samples,

### STRICT table validation preserves fractional writes

A native reproduction replaced value_num REAL with INTEGER in a STRICT
cave_claim table. Schema.check accepted it, but inserting 3.5 failed with
SQLite's datatype constraint. Ordinary numeric affinity is insufficient for
STRICT compatibility. SQLite also treats STRICT ANY as preserving storage
classes without coercion, unlike ordinary ANY's numeric affinity; the source
reference is https://www.sqlite.org/stricttables.html.

Schema validation now reads table metadata once and accounts for STRICT mode.
The four fraction-bearing fields (value_num, delta_num, sigma_level, conf) must
be REAL in a STRICT table. STRICT ANY does not count as numeric affinity for
integer-like fields either. Compatible standard STRICT declarations pass;
the generated schema remains non-STRICT, with no migration or version change.
This check does not certify arbitrary additional constraints or historical rows.

The shared regression first failed against the prior validator
(`/tmp/cave-strict-affinity-red.log`). It covers INTEGER/INT/ANY substitutions
for four fraction-bearing fields and ANY for three integer-like fields,

fractional value, delta, sigma and confidence. All 577 store/sync/website tests
pass on Node 24.21.0 and 26.8.1 (`/tmp/cave-strict-affinity{24,26}.log`).

### Cumulative explanation work has a calibrated runtime limit

The candidate cumulative accounting rule was calibrated before implementation
against ten existing workload invocations, each with unchanged correctness

variants, a near-numeric-budget sum, nine intermediate-growth cases and the

counts and source hashes. The same controls pass after implementation.

Limits.maxExplanationWork now defaults to 10,000,000 per report. At each
successful size preflight, the largest estimated bit bound is charged before
guarded arithmetic. An over-budget charge is refused without consuming the
remaining allowance. Hard and soft evaluations share it; cheap or previously
completed identical evaluations may still finish. Exhaustion leaves the backend
result intact and records a local maxExplanationWork reason. A new report resets
the counter. This is deterministic estimated arithmetic work, not elapsed time,
whole-process memory or all report phases. Size-limit precedence is tested both
with the default work allowance and with an explicitly enlarged allowance.

### Explanation reuse matches isolated evaluations across syntax families

A new differential regression compares one-constraint reports with a report
containing every predicate plus separately cloned duplicates in reverse order.
Its 298 predicate shapes exercise all expression operator families, integer and
real literal forms, two- and three-operand groups, numeric and Boolean
conditionals, enum domains and escaped enum text. Three assignment states and
two size budgets include missing assignments, zero divisors, size failures and
short-circuit branches.

For each of the six state/budget combinations, complete hard-constraint results
must match the isolated entries exactly, including IDs and failure reasons.
That compares 1,788 isolated evaluations with 3,576 combined-report entries per
runtime. No mismatch was found. This specifically checks report-cache isolation;
it is not an independent arithmetic oracle and does not establish a general
resource limit.

All 347 solver, Z3 and scenario tests pass on Node 24.21.0 and 26.8.1
(`/tmp/cave-explanation-isolation-full{24,26}.log`). Workspace typecheck,
production site build, all ten documentation checks, changeset metadata and
selected whitespace checks pass
(`/tmp/cave-explanation-isolation-{typecheck,site,docs}.log`). The solver guide
records the regression's scope. A solver patch changeset covers the test and

### Report-scoped evaluation reuse removes repeated rational sums

The cumulative-sum trial exposed roughly 30-second reports because identical
ordered predicates were evaluated separately for every declaration. The report
now caches each complete local Boolean result or evaluation-failure reason by an
iteratively constructed ordered syntax key. The cache belongs only to one
captured assignment and limit set; hard/soft declaration IDs, evidence,
descriptions and weights remain separate. Keys preserve operand order, arity,
literal representation and enum domains, avoiding the reordered operands of
model canonicalization. Large intermediate rationals are not retained.

The two new regressions check that identical hard/soft expressions execute
arithmetic guards only once, preserve distinct declaration metadata, and do not
reuse results across changed assignments or budgets. A second check preserves
missing-assignment versus division-by-zero reasons under reversed operand order,
short-circuit behavior and repeated failures. All 346 solver, Z3 and scenario
tests pass on Node 24.21.0 and 26.8.1 (`/tmp/cave-expression-reuse{24,26}.log`).

Both cumulative harnesses were then run sequentially, without concurrent builds

### Schema migrations preserve rollback failures alongside the original error

The migration catch block swallowed every rollback exception under the assumption
that SQLite might already have rolled back. This hid independent cleanup failures
from direct Schema.init callers and from failed store startup. The shared-adapter
regression fails against the previous implementation because it receives only the
migration Error, not the expected combined failure
(`/tmp/cave-migration-rollback-red.log`).

Schema.init now follows the ordinary store transaction contract: if rollback
throws, AggregateError.errors retains the original migration and rollback values
in order, Error.cause remains the migration failure, and the message includes
both diagnostics using safe formatting. Successful rollback keeps the existing
single-error wrapper. Tests cover a rollback rejected before execution, a failure
reported after rollback executes, and a second rollback after an automatic
rollback. They verify retained identities and retry after required cleanup, with
no partial schema or advanced version left behind. Automatic rollback can itself
produce the second diagnostic; the aggregate does not establish that a transaction
is still active. The guide documents that distinction and connection ownership.

(`/tmp/cave-migration-rollback{24,26}.log`). Workspace typecheck, website build,

### Invalid array lengths cannot become empty connector batches

An array proxy can pass Array.isArray while advertising NaN, a negative value
or a string as its length. The shared capture loop interpreted those values as
an empty batch, allowing direct pruning to retire existing records and SQL
projection to return a misleading empty source. The regression fails against
the previous implementation with a missing expected exception
(`/tmp/cave-array-length-red.log`).

Batch preflight now reads length once and requires a numeric integer in the
ordinary array-length range, 0 through 4,294,967,295. The regression rejects
nine invalid values through both direct connect and Source.queryRecords before
writes, verifies identical full annotated history, and retries a changing length
getter with its first valid value. The preserved record is skipped without
pruning; a subsequent valid empty batch still intentionally prunes it. This
validates the advertised array view, without promising a deep field snapshot
or detecting a proxy that deliberately advertises a different valid length.

### SQL projection shares batch validation and preserves record selection

Source.queryRecords discovered columns and inserted rows in separate traversals
of the caller's array. A changing index getter could supply a row with an ID for
column discovery and a different row without that ID for insertion. A normal
`WHERE id IS NOT NULL` projection then returned an empty source, and a subsequent
pruning connect pass incorrectly retired the original record. SQL staging also
accepted primitive entries as field-less rows instead of rejecting the malformed
record batch. Both regressions fail against the previous implementation
(`/tmp/cave-sql-record-capture-red.log`).

The direct connector's batch preflight is now a shared private helper, used by
Source.queryRecords before column discovery and staging. It captures array
entries without reading record fields, rejects malformed or sparse batches and
retains valid empty batches and field-less object rows. The integration regression
passes a changing array getter through a filtered SQL projection and then connect
with pruning enabled: the previous record is skipped unchanged, not pruned,
and full annotated history remains identical. Existing direct batch and field-
capture regressions still pass.

### Connector batch preflight protects pruning and record identity

The direct connect API did not validate the record-array structure before its
prelude and record writes. Array.forEach skipped holes, so a sparse input could
be treated as a smaller successful source and prune prior records whose entries
were missing. Other malformed entries could fail only after earlier writes.
With source spans, the array was also traversed once for provenance and again
for mapping, allowing a changing index getter to supply different records.
Both regressions fail against the previous implementation
(`/tmp/cave-connect-batch-red.log`).

Connect now validates a dense array of object records and captures its entries
before source provenance, prelude, mapping and pruning. Missing or inherited-only
slots, nulls, primitives and nested arrays are rejected with a record position;
non-array batches receive an array diagnostic. Field values retain their existing
lazy per-record capture, so this does not replace template field semantics with
a deep clone. Tests preserve full annotated history across every malformed batch,
including a changed prelude and enabled pruning; a corrected batch then prunes
the genuinely removed record and applies the prelude. Another test verifies one
index-getter read when source spans and mapping both consume the batch.

### Z3 deadline retries mitigate a reproduced pending-check stall

The prior 208.5-second Node 26 timeout test did not reproduce in a single focused
run (277 ms) or a full real-Z3 sequence (159 ms for that case; all 24 tests pass).
A new bounded diagnostic then ran three fresh processes with ten 1 ms pigeonhole
requests each, followed by a satisfiable recovery check on the same runtime.
One Node 26 process stalled during its sixth request and exceeded the parent's
15-second allowance. The parent terminated that process and retained partial
phase events; the other 25 requests completed in 118–191 ms. Logs are
`/tmp/cave-z3-deadline-{focused26.log,suite26.log,probe26.json}`.

The check deadline previously sent one interrupt only. Its private helper now
repeats cancellation every 50 ms after expiry until the asynchronous check

are conservative: cancellation may have produced a small answer, but the

hard/soft constraint-evaluation guard, not a time, heap or cumulative-work cap.
Copying, model validation, report formatting/soft-weight normalization, standalone
Exact helpers, linear classification and backend execution remain separate.

A refused operation becomes an indeterminate local evaluation with a
maxExplanationBits reason. Backend status, assignment and metadata remain intact;
independent constraints continue and skipped branches stay unevaluated. Increasing
the limit permits a fresh report to evaluate the same inputs. Existing saved
reports keep precisely their declared historical limits: validation accepts older
sets without inserting the new default into immutable recorded evidence.

### Balanced explanation products reduce repeated work on growing fractions

N-ary multiplication used a left fold even though all operands were already
captured and type-checked into an owned numeric array. Each step could combine
a small factor with a progressively larger fraction. A bounded trial multiplies
128, 1,024 or 4,096 independently constructed references to the assigned rational
1 + 10^-50 and checks that the product exceeds one. All models pass default
limits; the largest has 4,099 counted expression nodes and a 204,801-digit result
denominator. Before the change, median complete reports at that size took
1648.504 ms on Node 24.21.0 and 1623.321 ms on Node 26.8.1.

Multiplication now uses the existing balanced reducer, as addition already did.
The same trials take 40.996 and 37.995 ms, roughly 40 times faster. Operand
evaluation and numeric validation still happen before the zero identity and
reduction, preserving local failures rather than hiding undefined arithmetic.
This is exact associative arithmetic, not floating-point reassociation. It
improves the measured factor distribution without imposing a general work cap.
The standalone harness, before/after samples, source hashes and both-major
oracle results live in `scripts/solver-flat-product-bench.mjs` and
`benchmarks/explanation-flat-product-review.json`. Timings ran sequentially in
fresh children without competing builds or tests; their 30-second timeout and
256 MB V8 old-space allowance are harness controls, not library limits.

### Exact snapshots preserve semantic damage for independent recovery work

Review of `verifyBackup` confirmed its boundary: it checks SQLite integrity,
foreign keys, supported schema and an optional supplied checksum. It does not
recompute semantic claim identities or validate provenance values. Adding those
export/doctor checks to exact backup would prevent preserving a structurally
valid damaged store before recovery. The existing exact-copy behavior is
retained deliberately and is now explicit in the store and CLI guides.

A new lifecycle regression corrupts a claim key and inserts an empty provenance
value, then takes and verifies an exact snapshot. Restore publishes identical
snapshot bytes and preserves the original claim/context/provenance rows.
Annotated export on the restored copy first rejects the key; correcting only
the key then reveals the preserved provenance error. Correcting that value
permits export. Source rows and the snapshot checksum remain unchanged after
repairing the restored copy. This establishes preservation and independence,
not automatic semantic repair or a guarantee that all SQLite corruption can
be backed up.

removed wholesale. Two cases preserve the existing reduced-fraction invariant:
adding zero and adding an integer. For reduced `a/b`,

harness confirmed that adding one to the already optimized depth-12 product
still spent about 2.2 seconds reducing its result.

Explanation addition now returns the other value for zero, and directly builds
the reduced result when either operand has denominator one. Other sums retain
the existing sum-and-normalize path. The evaluator still obtains and checks
every operand before these identities apply; undefined arithmetic is not
skipped. Subtraction benefits through its existing use of addition.

unreduced supplied assignments, fractional denominators and exact cancellation.

known to be false, and every measured explanation reports it as violated.

### Doctor diagnoses historical claim-key disagreement with stored contexts

The previous annotated-export fix exposed a diagnostic gap: doctor decoded
stored claims without their context side table and never compared semantic
keys. A regression corrupting an older revision's key reported the store as

snapshot. It does not accumulate history, repair rows or expose private keys,

includes claim keys. Existing successful output and report schema are unchanged.

older revision, checks plain and JSON failures and byte-identical source files,
then repairs the fixture and verifies successful diagnosis with the legitimate
contexts intact. Packed CLI smoke separately adds a context without updating

### Annotated export preserves semantic identity as well as transaction identity

Historical rows can carry a `claim_key` that disagrees with their decoded claim.
Structured `recordOf` already rejects that mismatch, but annotated export did
not: it emitted the original transaction ID with text whose replay computed a
different key. This could move the transaction into a different belief series.
The new regression failed with “Missing expected exception” before the fix
(`/tmp/cave-export-key-red.log`).

For `tx: true`, export now recomputes the included claim's key, including its
contexts, inside the existing read snapshot and rejects a mismatch before
emission. Its located error retains the cause and identifies the claim without
including the incorrect key or private subject. This is validation, not a
repair. Plain semantic export retains its existing behavior. The regression
covers current and historical exports, sensitivity exclusion, unchanged source
rows, and exact export recovery after restoring the correct key. The CLI
regression additionally preserves an existing output file and database bytes,
then verifies that corrected export/sync restores both transaction ID and key.
The packed consumer smoke exercises rejection and repair too.

caller-cached evaluator and sign proof are private shared modules. The product

undefined divisor or an assignment reference. Unknown signs, mixed-sign
cancellation, variables and conditionals fall back to ordinary exact evaluation.

Boolean short-circuiting and local error diagnostics. No public API changes.

### Fusion cancellation matches an independent integer oracle

The exact fallback now has an independent oracle over 768 deterministic ordered
cases. Each fixture uses small signed multiples of MIN_VALUE, uncertainties
from 1, 2, 4 and 8, and confidences from 1, 1/4 and 1/16. Scaling all weights by
1024 yields exact small integers. Opposite large estimates cancel analytically,
so expected means come from rounding a small rational number of MIN_VALUE units
with ties to even. This oracle does not reuse binary64 decomposition, BigInt
accumulation or the fusion implementation to derive expected means.

The matrix varies one or two cancelling pairs, magnitudes of 1 or MAX_VALUE,
and three orders. Every result matches the expected signed mean and posterior
precision within the precision check's stated relative tolerance. The first
sigma-only trial and expanded confidence trial both pass; no new runtime
change is justified by this review. The guide records the oracle and limits:
this is bounded cancellation coverage, not a guarantee over arbitrary inputs
or unit-conversion rounding.

### Fusion overflow fallback retains subnormal cancellation residuals

Four equally weighted extreme means (`MAX_VALUE`, `MAX_VALUE`, `-MAX_VALUE`,
`-MAX_VALUE`) cancel, but the previous fusion calculation returned zero when
five `MIN_VALUE` means remained. The exact average of those nine inputs rounds
to `MIN_VALUE`. Its unnormalized numerator overflowed, and the separate
normalized contributions lost the tiny residuals before summation. A new
regression failed on the old implementation at this boundary.

When the compensated numerator is non-finite, fusion now represents the finite
binary64 means and normalized root-weight factors as integers at a shared
binary scale, accumulates their products, and rounds the quotient once to the
nearest representable double, ties to even. This also retains contributions
that underflow if each weighted product is rounded separately. The ordinary
finite compensated path remains unchanged. Unit conversion, root-weight
calculation and the whole posterior are not made exact; the guide states that
scope. The fallback adds integer arithmetic only at this overflow boundary.

Two regressions cover positive and negative residuals, input orders, zero at a
halfway subnormal boundary, unequal weights, and a normal-sized final result.

### Automation stdin cleanup retains input and resource failures

The declaration reader previously called pause and removed its listeners in one
unguarded cleanup function. A throwing pause or listener removal interrupted
cleanup, escaped an input callback and could leave the read promise pending.
The reader now settles once, attempts every cleanup operation independently,
and rejects with the original error or an AggregateError retaining all failures
in order, with the first as cause. Data/end callbacks ignore later invocations.
A cleanup failure after ordinary EOF prevents buffered declarations from being
ingested; cancellation plus cleanup failure remains an error rather than quiet
cancellation. The owning command-input guide now states these boundaries.

Three regression cases cover input error, normal EOF and cancellation with a
throwing pause and data-listener removal after their real operations. Each checks
no escaped callback failure, diagnostics for every error, detached stream/signal
listeners, no persisted buffered prefix and a successful new invocation after
correcting the input. The input-error case failed against the former code with
an escaped pause error (`/tmp/cave-stdin-cleanup-red-confirmed.log`); an initial
trial had a test-harness error and is not the defect evidence.

All 127 automation tests pass on Node 24.21.0 and 26.8.1
(`/tmp/cave-stdin-cleanup24.log`, `/tmp/cave-stdin-cleanup26.log`). Typechecking,
root and consolidated CLI builds, website build and all ten documentation checks
pass in `/tmp/cave-stdin-cleanup-{typecheck,build,cli,site,docs}.log`.

### Zero detection validates without normalizing magnitudes

Exact.isZero previously normalized a complete rational just to inspect its
numerator. Nonzero fraction fields incurred BigInt parsing, GCD and serialization
work; decimal inputs could allocate enormous expansions despite the predicate
needing only the coefficient. The predicate now validates integer numerator and
denominator fields without reducing them, rejecting zero denominators even for
zero numerators. Field reads remain single and ordered: invalid numerators fail
before denominator getters. Decimal strings share the normalizer's syntax and
safe-integer exponent validation, then inspect the coefficient without expansion.
Thus valid enormous exponents can be classified without allocating their value;
this does not change model limits or make normalization of that value practical.
Linearity analysis benefits when it checks an already evaluated constant divisor.

Two deterministic regressions failed before the change
(`/tmp/cave-zero-detection-red.log`). They now cover no large BigInt parsing,
invalid denominators, single field capture and failure order, decimal signs,
coefficients, bounded cross-checks against normalization, enormous valid exponents
and malformed/unsafe exponents. All 304 solver, Z3 and scenario tests pass on
Node 24.21.0 and 26.8.1 (`/tmp/cave-zero-detection24.log`,
`/tmp/cave-zero-detection26.log`).

Sequential standalone `scripts/exact-zero-bench.mjs` runs compare the predicate
with full rational normalization at 1,000/100,000/1,000,000-digit denominators,
using zero and nonzero numerators, two warmups and seven measured samples.
One-million-digit nonzero-fraction medians change from 208.396 to 0.779 ms on
Node 24 and 206.269 to 0.778 ms on Node 26. Zero controls remain about 0.39 ms;
their small differences are not a speedup claim. All samples and runtime/platform
metadata are in `benchmarks/exact-zero-review.json`. The solver guide and benchmark

### Canonical integer order avoids reparsing large magnitudes

Arithmetic review found that Exact.compare reparsed already normalized integer
text into BigInts even when a shortcut could determine the order without
cross-products. The new private integer-order helper compares canonical sign,
digit length and lexical order. Both rationals still normalize and validate
before shortcuts. Equal denominators, zeros, opposite signs, equal numerators
and reinforcing numerator/denominator orders use text comparisons; the general
cross-product path still allocates BigInts. Fraction normalization may itself
parse magnitudes and compute GCDs. This is an allocation/work reduction, not a
general input or intermediate arithmetic budget.

A deterministic regression failed before the change because large decimal
magnitudes were reparsed (`/tmp/cave-exact-text-red.log`). It now checks positive,
negative, equal, opposite-sign, zero and different-length integers without a
large BigInt conversion and still rejects an invalid second operand. Existing
signed-fraction comparisons against independent cross-products remain green.

(`/tmp/cave-exact-text24.log`, `/tmp/cave-exact-text26.log`).

The reproducible `scripts/exact-integer-order-bench.mjs` compares integer decimal
inputs against normalized-numerator BigInt reparsing, including normalization in

independent of the store.

### Z3 shutdown awaits worker exits before clearing handlers

Run-policy verification exposed an existing intermittent process-exit failure:
Emscripten reported a cleanupThread command from an already terminated worker.
The old close path waited one timer turn before terminating the pool and
replacing message handlers. That delay could not establish that pending worker
messages had been delivered. The pool can also retain persistent workers after
a check, so waiting for runningWorkers to become empty is not a valid shutdown
condition.

Shutdown now requests Node worker termination and awaits exit acknowledgments
before Emscripten clears the pool and replaces its handlers. Pending messages
keep their normal handlers until exit; newly observed workers are included
before final pool teardown. This handles running and idle workers without
suppressing stderr or relaxing the real process-exit assertion. Three owning
regressions cover deferred worker exits, movement between pool lists, workers
created by pending messages, and empty/absent pools. The old timer algorithm
fails the new regression fixture. Twenty short-lived Node 26 solver processes
then exit successfully with empty stderr.

The final source passes all 300 solver/Z3/scenario tests on Node 24.21.0 and
26.8.1, including close/reopen lifecycle checks and the new run-policy checks.
Root build, CLI consolidation, website build and all ten documentation checks
pass. All 12 public packages pass installed smoke, including optional Z3 worker
shutdown and run-policy rejection. NodeNext/Bundler imports pass; the API
snapshot includes the preceding explanationContext validator export and needs
no additional shutdown API change. The Z3 guide documents exit acknowledgments
and persistent-worker handling. General book lifecycle guidance remains
accurate. This change postdates both full integration runs.

### Solver outcomes require explicit proof markers

The adapter contract requires literal proof markers for optimal and unsatisfied
outcomes, but result wrappers previously trusted those fields without runtime
checks. A malformed adapter could therefore produce a report labelled optimal
or unsatisfied with a missing or false proof marker. Unsupported status values
could also leave a report without an outcome. The first two new regressions
failed before the fix (`/tmp/cave-result-proof-red.log`).

A shared internal result capture now copies the adapter result and checks its
status and required proof marker. `Solve.run`, `Solve.runWithExplanation` and
direct `Explain.report` reject missing, false or coerced markers with TypeError;
unsupported statuses also fail. A changing getter is read once, and the checked
snapshot is the value subsequently returned or explained. Solve.run now returns
an owned copy. This enforces the adapter assertion contract, not proof correctness
or comprehensive validation/resource limits for other result fields.

All 273 solver, Z3 and scenario tests pass on Node 24.21.0 and Node 26.8.1
(`/tmp/cave-result-proof24.log`, `/tmp/cave-result-proof26.log`). CLI build,
website build and all ten documentation checks pass
(`/tmp/cave-result-proof-build.log`, `/tmp/cave-result-proof-site.log`,
`/tmp/cave-result-proof-docs.log`). The solver guide documents the new failure
behavior and ownership contract; a solver patch changeset records it. Earlier

### Real URL timeouts cover stalled bodies and fresh retries

combined timeout signal through built-in fetch, but the existing real-server
regression exercised caller cancellation rather than timeout expiry. This pass

confirms headers arrived before the request fails, the request signal carries a
`TimeoutError`, and no partial document or digest is returned. A fresh call to

implementations honor their supplied signal.

### Text sync reuses stored identities across repeated graph references

Text-sync validation reread and canonically rendered the same stored row for
every repeated graph reference. A local Node 26.8.1 trial replaying 5,000
references to one existing row with explicit provenance measured a 229.21 ms
median over five measured runs after one warm-up
(`/tmp/cave-sync-repeat-before.json`; driver `/tmp/cave-sync-repeat-bench.mjs`).

Added a cache scoped to the reserved validation call for stored canonical
identity and lazily needed provenance, including absent identities. Every
incoming occurrence still computes and compares its own content/provenance;
only the unchanged stored side is reused. Rendering mismatches retain the prior
short-circuit behavior before provenance lookup. The guide documents the cache's
lifetime and memory proportional to unique input identities, without claiming an
overall replay memory cap.

The prototype median was 97.03 ms (`/tmp/cave-sync-repeat-after.json`); a fresh
trial of the final code measured 120.16 ms (`/tmp/cave-sync-repeat-final.json`),
about 48% below the baseline. These sequential local trials demonstrate this
repeated-reference workload, not a universal speedup or formal performance bound.
Regression coverage exercises 2,001 occurrences with bare-then-explicit
provenance, late content/provenance conflicts with unchanged target state, and
new identity replay followed by idempotent repetition across separate calls.

### URL context lookup finds percent-encoded source names

Reviewed the ingestion context lookup and store search boundary. Store search
quotes literal tokens by default, but URL-derived tokens still contained their
percent encoding. A URL ending in `caf%C3%A9.md` therefore failed to select an
existing `café USES auth` claim as related context. The regression failed before
